museumData.title: Gikuyu Cultural Heritage Collection
museumData.description: Comprehensive collection of Gikuyu (Agikuyu/Kikuyu) cultural artifacts, stories, traditions, and historical information from Central Kenya

communityOverview.traditionalTerritory: Around Mount Kenya, including Murang'a, Nyeri, Kiambu, Nyandarua, Kirinyaga and Nakuru counties
communityOverview.historicalSignificance: Championed Kenya's independence through the Mau Mau movement and Kikuyu Central Association (KCA)
notableFigures: Mzee Jomo Kenyatta - First President of Kenya (1963-1978)
Professor Wangari Maathai - Nobel Peace Prize recipient

artifacts.name: Gicandi
artifacts.description: An ancient Gikuyu composition of enigmatic poetry presented in public by two poets in a dialogue of back and forth battle of wits. Composed of reportedly over 150 stanzas, the Gicandi is both a musical instrument and a mnemonic-pictorial system.
artifacts.culturalSignificance: The epitome of creative expression in Gikuyu culture. The Gicandi singer (Muini wa Gicandi) is considered the Grand Master, representing the highest level of intellectual and artistic achievement.
artifacts.performance: Two contestants would propose enigmas in turn, with the competition continuing until one failed to give the interpretation and lost the game. The losing party handed over his musical instrument to the winner.
artifacts.uniqueFeature: The drawings on the Gicandi are as enigmatic as the words and constitute a mnemonic-pictorial system that is the only kind existent among the Bantu tribes, reminiscent of hieroglyphics writing system of ancient Egypt
artifacts.documentation: Vittorio Merlo Pick, an Italian Consolata missionary, recorded 126 of originally 150 stanzas with John Kahora in 1930 in the book 'Ndai na Gicandi: Kikuyu Enigmas'

artifacts.name: Gataki
artifacts.description: A traditional Gikuyu artifact shown in the collection

artifacts.name: Mwano (Divination Gourd)
artifacts.description: The most important gourd in the medicine man's arsenal, used for divination and containing medicine to heal the sick. It has a long neck, decorated with a woven leather strap and plant fibre handle, sealed with a plant fibre lid attached with leather to the neck.
artifacts.culturalSignificance: Primary apparatus of the medicine man (mundu mugo), who was a powerful person in the community consulted about the future, for healing and cleansing from ill omens
artifacts.materials: Gourd, woven leather strap, plant fibre

artifacts.name: Ndome (Dancing Shield)
artifacts.description: Shields carved out of a single piece of wood, with a hole for the arm instead of a hand grip, worn on the upper left arm. Used by boys prior to their initiation as junior warriors.
artifacts.culturalSignificance: Each year boys of a particular territorial unit would choose a design, which they later used for their war shields once they achieved warrior status. These became family heirlooms, though designs might be scraped off and repainted many times as each new generation prepared for initiation.

artifacts.name: Kahiu ka Irima (Digging Knife)
artifacts.description: Traditional digging knife with a wooden handle carved from Murembu wood, made by blacksmiths at Kirwara.
artifacts.use: Used by women for cultivating fields, clearing bushes, weeding and harvesting cassava and sweet potatoes

artifacts.name: Kiondo (Basket)
artifacts.description: A woven basket made in various shapes, colors, and sizes, decorated with geometric designs. Strings for making baskets were gathered from the bark of several indigenous shrubs.
artifacts.culturalSignificance: Notable traditional economic activity among Agikuyu women
artifacts.uses: Apart from weaving baskets and trays, the strings were also used in making snares, repairing calabashes, stringing beads or tying loads

artifacts.name: Riumba Cooking Pot
artifacts.description: Kikuyu pot with a straight neck and rim decorated with diagonal lines, made using a mixture of three types of clay – red, white and black – obtained from swamps and along river banks.
artifacts.uses: Used for cooking, storing grain, carrying water and for trade
artifacts.production: Women collected and made these pots under the shade, in a similar manner to the Kamba

artifacts.name: Wooden Food Bowl
artifacts.description: Wooden food bowl made by a craftsman, used by everybody for eating dry foods

artifacts.name: Ceremonial Headdress
artifacts.description: A headdress made from sisal ropes which were dyed with castor oil
artifacts.use: Used by Kikuyu elders during ceremonial occasions

artifacts.name: Fly Whisk
artifacts.description: Made using a cow tail, fitted firmly with a wooden handle
artifacts.culturalSignificance: Made by men and carried by elders as a symbol of status

artifacts.name: Wandindi (Fiddle)
artifacts.description: The fiddle is played by a specialist using a sisal stringed bow (muthage). The specialist would go round the countryside playing the instrument and singing in markets and at dances.

artifacts.name: Kigamba (Large Leg Rattles)
artifacts.description: Large rattles made by blacksmiths and worn by travelers and dancers just below the knee during special occasions such as war dances, initiation ceremonies and other ceremonial dances. Made with four long bells sewn on a thick pad of leather.
artifacts.use: Worn by older men for dancing
artifacts.modernVersion: Today, such bells are made from scrap iron and ball bearings

culturalPractices.name: Cengerecema
culturalPractices.description: A famous mind game strictly for Kikuyu neophytes used to develop and train memory, wit, shrewdness, richness of imagination, and the spirit of observation.
culturalPractices.text:
Witagwo atia? – Cengerecema
Ii cema? – Cema uuthi
Ii uuthi? – Uuthi kagira
Ii kagira? – Kagira nyenje
Ii nyenje – Nyenje wairi
Ii wairi? – Wairi uri nda
Ii nda? – Nda ya mwene
Ii mwene? – Mwene matote
Ii matote?- Matotera thi
Ii thi? – Thi ya murogi
Ii murogi? – Murogi ciari
Ii ciari? – Ciari gatara
Ii gatara? – Gatara hungu
Ii hungu? – Hungu king'uu
Ii king'uu? – King'uira iguru
culturalPractices.culturalContext: Part of the educational system where young people progressed from riddles to more complex linguistic and poetic forms
culturalPractices.progression: Young grew up with mind games, fairy tales, riddles and enigmas, then adults deepened these skills in music and poetry like Muthunguci, Mugoiyo and Gicukia

culturalPractices.name: Irua (Initiation/Circumcision)
culturalPractices.description: The Agikuyu circumcised both boys and girls at puberty. As an important cultural practice, circumcision was characterized by celebration.
culturalPractices.significance: Circumcised girls became women ready for marriage, and boys became warriors. Initiates circumcised at the same time formed an age-set (riika).
culturalPractices.modernContext: In Kenya today, female circumcision is illegal and communities are encouraged to adopt alternative initiation rites which do not involve female genital mutilation

culturalPractices.name: Nguracio (Traditional Marriage Ceremony)
culturalPractices.description: When a young man found a suitable woman to marry, he was expected to pay bride wealth (ruracio) to her family. Parents of both bride and groom engaged in discussions, exchanged gifts, and assessed whether the couple were a suitable match.
culturalPractices.process: Elders and fathers of the groom and bride drank locally brewed beer (muratina) together as they negotiated for bride wealth (sheep, goats and cattle). A man could marry as many wives as he could afford.
culturalPractices.celebration: Characterized by a great feast, songs, dance and merry-making

culturalPractices.name: Kiama (Council of Elders)
culturalPractices.description: The council of elders was responsible for ensuring law and order, decision-making, ritual oath taking, religion, and administration.
culturalPractices.authority: The kiama presided over all issues concerning the community as a whole
culturalPractices.culturalSignificance: Known for proverbs-rich rhetoric. As stated in Kahora's stanza 17: 'While the warriors divide their hairs, and the young boys talk about goats, the elders discuss the secrets of the Council (ndundu cia ciira).'

traditionalFoods.name: Irio
traditionalFoods.description: Mashed dry beans, corn and potatoes

traditionalFoods.name: Mutura
traditionalFoods.description: Sausage made using goat intestines, meat and blood

traditionalFoods.name: Ucuru
traditionalFoods.description: Fermented porridge made from flour of corn, millet or sorghum

traditionalFoods.name: Muratina
traditionalFoods.description: Locally brewed beer used in ceremonies and negotiations

supremeBeing.name: Ngai
supremeBeing.worship: Prayers and sacrifices at designated places such as on top of hills, Mount Kenya and under specific trees (especially fig/Mugumo trees)
supremeBeing.sacrifices: Conducted by members of the ruling generation, who appoint special priests for each occasion

creationMyth.landGrant: Ngai allotted Gikuyu all land south-west of Mount Kenya (currently Kirinyaga county)
creationMyth.sacredPlace: Mukurwe wa Nyagathanga in Murang'a - a gazetted cultural site with many fig trees
creationMyth.clanOrigin: Nine men appeared under the mugumo tree who married the daughters and became the ancestors of the nine Kikuyu clans

historicalFigures.name: Mugo wa Kibiru (Cege wa Kibiru)
historicalFigures.title: The Great Seer/Prophet
historicalFigures.description: A famous Gikuyu healer and prophet man who was found alone in the forest by a hunter called Kibiru. His parents are unknown.
historicalFigures.clan: Anjiru clan (traditionally associated with prophecy and powerful medicine)
historicalFigures.abilities: Possessed powers to control animals, occasionally claimed to have been with God (Ngai)
prophecies: Coming of the white man with skin like pale frogs (Kiengere)
White men carrying fire in their pockets (matchboxes)
Cooked food being sold by roadside
Maasai grazing plains turned into farmland
Kenya-Uganda railway (iron snake with many legs that swallowed and spat out white men)
A fig tree in Thika that would die only after white men left the country 68 years after colonization
historicalFigures.imageReference: Shujaa Stories illustration by National Museums of Kenya

historicalFigures.name: Karuri wa Gakure
historicalFigures.title: The Great Chief
historicalFigures.family: Father from Angari clan, mother named Wangari
historicalFigures.description: A famous Kikuyu medicine man and warrior who displayed leadership qualities among his peers from a young age.
activities: Hunted elephants for ivory to trade with Arabs
Became medicine man (bought herbs for thirty goats from Githaiga wa Muya, Gikemi wa Karura and hunter-gathering communities)
Led Kikuyu warriors to battle after giving them medicine believed to make them invincible
historicalFigures.imageReference: Shujaa Stories illustration by National Museums of Kenya

traditional.evolved: Later adopted agriculture as main source of livelihood

genderRoles.women: Farming and gathering of wild fruits using traditional tools (hoes, digging knives) for domestic consumption

traditional.learned: Learnt the art of iron-making and smelting from the Gumba people

ironWorking.products: Knives and weapons from iron ore dug out of ground and smelted
ironWorking.trade: In markets, tobacco, vegetables, skins and gourds were exchanged for iron, pottery, leather garments, salt and red ochre

basketMaking.products: Kiondo baskets in various shapes, colors and sizes with geometric designs

pottery.material: Riumba (special clay from swamps and river banks)
pottery.products: Pots for cooking, storing grain, carrying water and trade

socialOrganization.ageSets: Riika (initiates circumcised at the same time)

migrationHistory.origin: Ancestors arrived in Kenya and settled on slopes of Mount Kenya
migrationHistory.indigenous: Found the Gumba people whom they assimilated
migrationHistory.gumba: Hunters who made iron and pottery, used honey and honey products
migrationHistory.expansion: As population increased, dispersed to different areas around slopes of Mount Kenya
